featuredArticles.title: Navigating CBAM: Critical Preparation Steps for Non-EU Manufacturers
featuredArticles.summary: How industrial exporters can assess embedded emissions, avoid default values, and build resilient reporting pipelines before definitive implementation phases.
content: The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) represents a major structural shift in global trade and climate policy. Designed to equalize the carbon price paid by European domestic producers under the EU ETS and foreign producers exporting to the European single market, CBAM requires meticulous carbon accounting across covered goods including steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, and electricity.

For manufacturers and exporters outside the European Union, the immediate challenge centers on embedded emissions calculation. Default values provided by the European Commission are punitive and will lead to higher financial liabilities once certificate purchasing commences. Establishing actual supplier-specific greenhouse gas accounting is the single most effective way to protect commercial margins.

Green Gate Advisory recommends that exporting enterprises implement a 4-step readiness framework: (1) Confirm tariff classification and HS codes; (2) Demarcate installation boundaries and direct vs indirect energy inputs; (3) Engage Tier-1 precursors suppliers for verified emissions data; and (4) Establish automated quarterly data collation protocols to avoid trade friction.

featuredArticles.title: Article 6 and the Voluntary Market: Convergence, Integrity, and ITMOs
featuredArticles.summary: Analyzing the operational interface between Article 6.2 bilateral agreements, Corresponding Adjustments, and high-integrity voluntary carbon credits.
content: As Article 6 of the Paris Agreement moves into active bilateral implementation, carbon project developers face a bifurcated market. On one side are Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) authorized under Article 6.2 or 6.4 with Corresponding Adjustments; on the other are non-adjusted credits utilized for voluntary corporate claims.

Understanding the regulatory architecture of host countries is now mandatory for developers. A project's financial model cannot rely purely on historical voluntary market assumptions; it must account for whether host country governments will authorize credits for international transfer or retain them toward their own Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).

High-integrity project preparation requires early baseline screening, robust additionality tests that surpass national policy targets, and community benefit-sharing agreements that withstand international regulatory scrutiny.

featuredArticles.title: Structuring Bankable Climate Proposals for Multilateral Facilities
featuredArticles.summary: Key elements of climate rationale, theories of change, and financial structuring required by international funds including the GCF and GEF.
content: Securing concessional capital from multilateral climate funds like the Green Climate Fund (GCF) or Global Environment Facility (GEF) remains an intensive, evidence-driven process. The primary bottleneck is rarely financial desire, but the technical robustness of the project's climate rationale.

A successful proposal must establish an explicit causal link: demonstrating clearly how climate change is altering local conditions, why the proposed intervention is fundamentally a climate solution rather than traditional development assistance, and how economic sustainability will be maintained beyond the disbursement window.

Integrating environmental and social safeguards (ESS), gender action planning, and measurable monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) matrices from day one is essential to avoid multi-year revision cycles.

faqs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faqs.subtitle: Clear answers regarding advisory scope, credentials, regulatory procedures, and outcomes.

items.q: What does a climate advisory consultancy do?
items.a: A climate advisory consultancy helps organisations understand climate-related risks, regulations, funding opportunities and project options. Depending on the scope, support may include climate strategy, carbon markets, climate finance, emissions accounting, policy advice and implementation planning.

items.q: What is CBAM and why might exporters need to assess it?
items.a: The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism is a regulatory framework concerning the embedded emissions of certain imported goods. Exporters and supply-chain businesses may need to determine whether their products and commercial relationships fall within the applicable rules and what data or reporting processes are required.

items.q: What is an emissions trading system (ETS)?
items.a: An emissions trading system is a carbon-pricing mechanism in which regulated entities may need to manage emissions allowances under the rules of a particular scheme. Scope, obligations and procedures differ by jurisdiction.

items.q: Can Green Gate Advisory help develop a carbon credit project?
items.a: Green Gate Advisory’s proposed service scope includes opportunity screening, feasibility, methodology assessment, project documentation and MRV planning, as well as support through relevant validation, registration and commercialisation processes. Actual requirements and outcomes depend on project eligibility, programme rules and independent review.

items.q: What support is available for climate finance proposals?
items.a: Depending on eligibility and programme requirements, support may include opportunity mapping, concept note development, climate rationale, theory of change, logical framework, budgets, safeguards, gender considerations and monitoring plans.

items.q: Does Green Gate Advisory guarantee funding or carbon credit issuance?
items.a: No. Funding decisions, validation, verification, registration and issuance are determined by the relevant funders, standards, registries or independent bodies. Advisory support can help improve project preparation but cannot guarantee approval or issuance.

items.q: Can training be tailored to our organisation?
items.a: Training topics, depth, format and duration can be discussed based on the audience, prior knowledge, institutional objectives and intended learning outcomes.

sections.body: We apply technical measures to safeguard submissions. Information is retained only as long as necessary to fulfill the initial advisory dialogue or comply with applicable legal recordkeeping rules.

sections.title: Your Rights
sections.body: You have the right to request access to, rectification of, or erasure of your personal details at any time by contacting our privacy team at privacy@greengateadvisory.com.
